```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(agecraft)
```

An `age_group` vector defines intervals. An `age_scheme` packages that vector
with an identifier, purpose, provenance, and validation rules. Store the scheme
once and reuse it across observations. It is an S3 metadata object containing
an interval vector, rather than another vector class attached to every age.

## A user-defined five-year partition

Intervals include their lower bound and exclude their upper bound: `[0,5)`
contains ages below 5, including fractions such as 4.9. A partition disallows
overlapping groups. Completeness is a separate claim against a declared domain.

```{r partition}
cuts <- c(seq(0, 85, by = 5), Inf)
g <- age_group(head(cuts, -1), tail(cuts, -1), unit = "year")
names(g) <- as.character(g)
five_year <- age_scheme(
  g, id = "example_five_year", name = "Illustrative five-year bands",
  domain = c(0, Inf), complete = TRUE,
  purpose = "Example population tabulation"
)
five_year
summary(five_year)
head(as.data.frame(five_year))
```

A domain uses the same unit as the intervals. Use `complete = NA` when making
no completeness claim. An incomplete partition can be useful: disjoint groups
covering ages 0–17 need not cover the rest of a declared all-age domain. With
`complete = FALSE`, construction verifies that coverage really is incomplete.
Without a domain, coverage and domain gaps are unspecified.

```{r classification}
a <- age(c(0, 4.9, 5, 84.9, 85, NA), unit = "year")
categorize_age(a, by = five_year)
categorize_age(a, by = five_year, output = "interval")
```

Classification uses stored fractions, regardless of the completed units shown
when printing an `age` vector. Plain numbers have no declared unit: wrap known
year values with `age(x, unit = "year")`. Schemes do not silently treat them as
years. Existing explicit conversion and approximate-conversion guards apply.

## Valid unit-bearing observations

An age must carry one supported simple time unit: second, minute, hour, day,
week, month or year. Common aliases, including the `units` representations
`s`, `min`, `h` and `d`, are accepted. Plain numeric observations can be given
a known meaning explicitly with `age(x, unit = "year")`; `age()` and numeric
`as_age()` default to years. A `units` object already expresses a quantity and
must have a valid time unit before it can be converted or classified.

`as_age()`, `categorize_age()`, `age_cat_iv()` and `classify_age_scheme()` reject
compound expressions such as `year/day`, squared units such as `year^2`, inverse
units such as `1/day`, dimensionless quantities (including time ratios), and
non-time quantities such as meters or kilograms. Unsupported time units such as
milliseconds must first be explicitly converted with `units` to a supported
simple unit. Validation checks the entire stored expression before numeric
extraction or a same-unit shortcut. Missing values and empty vectors do not
exempt their units from validation. Neither an explicit target unit nor
`allow_approx = TRUE` overrides the dimensional requirement.

```{r simple-time-units}
x <- units::set_units(c(0.5, 5, NA), "year")
categorize_age(x, by = five_year)
# categorize_age(units::set_units(0.5, "year/day"), by = five_year)
# errors: an age must have a supported simple time unit
```

## Floating-point boundaries

Age values are stored as double-precision numbers. Unit conversions can round
these values, including conversions between elapsed-time units with exact scale
relationships. When an observation is extremely close to a category boundary,
converting ages to group units can classify differently from converting group
boundaries to age units. For example, with the conversion backend used here:

```{r floating-point-boundary}
g <- age_group(c(0, 11), c(11, Inf), unit = "second")
names(g) <- c("Under eleven", "Eleven or more")
seconds <- age_scheme(g, "seconds", "Second categories")
x <- as_age(age(11, unit = "second"), unit = "day")
sprintf("%.17g", as.numeric(as_age(x, unit = "second")))
# "10.999999999999998"
classify_age_scheme(x, seconds, convert_units = "age_to_group")$label
# "Under eleven"
classify_age_scheme(x, seconds, convert_units = "group_to_age")$label
# "Eleven or more"
```

In the first path the converted observation is below 11 seconds; in the second,
the converted boundary equals the stored day value. This floating-point effect
also applies to `categorize_age()` and `age_cat_iv()`. Intervals retain exact
half-open `[start, end)` semantics in the matching coordinates, with no implicit
numerical tolerance or snapping of nearby values.

Use consistent units for observations and definitions when precise boundary
classification matters. `convert_units = "none"` prevents additional
classification-time conversion by rejecting different units. It cannot recover
precision already lost: converting `x` back to seconds first still leaves it below
11 on this backend. Supplying `age(11, unit = "second")` directly and classifying
with `"none"` includes it in "Eleven or more". See `?age` for the shared precision
policy; calendar approximation is a separate issue described next.

## Calendar conversion and exact classification

Calendar months and years use different anniversary intervals. A fractional
calendar year is measured between birthdays; a fractional calendar month is
measured between month anniversaries. Multiplying a year coordinate by twelve
does not generally reconstruct the month coordinate from the original dates.

Conversions between month and year now require `allow_approx = TRUE` in
`as_age()`, `categorize_age()`, `age_cat_iv()`, and `classify_age_scheme()`.
The same opt-in remains required between either calendar unit and elapsed-time
units. Matching units and conversions among elapsed-time units keep their
existing behavior. The guard applies whether observations or group boundaries
are converted (`convert_units = "age_to_group"` or `"group_to_age"`).

```{r calendar-conversion}
birth <- as.Date("2021-02-01")
reference <- as.Date("2021-03-01")
months <- calculate_age(birth, reference, unit = "month")
years <- calculate_age(birth, reference, unit = "year")
g <- age_group(c(0, 1), c(1, Inf), unit = "month")
names(g) <- c("Under one month", "One month or older")
monthly <- age_scheme(g, "example_monthly", "Illustrative monthly bands")
as.numeric(months) # 1 calendar month
as.numeric(as_age(years, "month", allow_approx = TRUE)) # about 0.921
classify_age_scheme(months, monthly)$label # One month or older
# classify_age_scheme(years, monthly) errors: conversion needs original dates
classify_age_scheme(years, monthly, allow_approx = TRUE)$label # Under one month
```

`allow_approx = TRUE` permits the existing numerical unit-factor conversion;
it does not recalculate calendar age or make the result calendar-exact. Near
category boundaries, classifications can therefore differ from calculations
performed directly in the target unit. For exact calendar classification,
calculate age from the original birth and reference dates in the scheme's unit.
The lightweight `age` vector stores values and a unit, so it cannot recover those
dates. This safeguard also applies to `units` inputs whose calculation basis is
unknown. Existing month/year conversion calls must explicitly opt in if numerical
conversion is intended.

## An overlapping classification

The following bands are invented to illustrate overlapping memberships. They
are not an official WHO, CDC, or clinical definition.

```{r overlap}
g <- age_group(c(10, 15, 10), c(20, 25, 25), unit = "year")
names(g) <- c("Example A", "Example B", "Example C")
overlapping <- age_scheme(
  g, id = "example_overlap", name = "Illustrative overlapping bands",
  type = "classification", domain = c(10, 25), complete = TRUE,
  notes = "Invented example; not an authoritative life-stage definition"
)
classify_age_scheme(age(c(12, 17, 24, 30, NA), unit = "year"), overlapping)
```

The long table has one row per membership. `observation` refers to the original
input position, and `group_index` to the original group order. Missing ages and
present-but-unmatched ages have separate statuses and one placeholder row each.
The `group` column contains matched intervals in the scheme's original units.
Interval-valued observations match only if fully contained in a category.

`categorize_age()` continues to error on multiple matches by default. An explicit
`multiple = "first"` or `"last"` selects one match in sorted interval order.
Overlapping categories cannot be summed as if they were mutually exclusive
population bands. A crosswalk also cannot determine how counts in a broad band
should be split into finer bands without additional data or assumptions.

## A legacy surveillance scheme

```{r registry}
list_age_schemes()[, c("id", "preset", "unit", "verified")]
ili <- get_age_scheme("legacy_ili")
ili
categorize_age(age(c(2, 15, 40, 70), unit = "year"), by = ili)
ili$source
ili$notes
```

All eight historical numeric presets have equivalent year-based schemes. The
numeric `age_group_presets` list and its `age.groups` alias remain unchanged.
The registry preserves their original boundaries and records source uncertainty;
these legacy bands are not verified current clinical or surveillance standards.
A package-snapshot version identifies the preserved definition, not an official
external edition. New authoritative definitions require source verification.

## Inspecting and changing a definition

Use `scheme_groups()` for the underlying intervals, `summary()` for coverage,
gaps, overlaps and provenance, and `as.data.frame()` for an inspection table.
The table has a `scheme_metadata` attribute; ordinary data-frame transformations
may discard it. Reconstruct with `age_scheme()` to validate a modified definition.
Do not retain claims of official source identity after changing cut points.

The constructor checks metadata and any declared coverage claim. A user-supplied
`verified = TRUE` requires source, reference, and version; it records the user's
claim, rather than performing external verification. Classification and inspection
revalidate the complete stored interval representation, including actual display
symbols, units, category names and endpoint fields, so direct list mutation
cannot silently bypass structural or declared-coverage checks. Missing or
malformed metadata is rejected without replacement by defaults. Custom scalar
strings for `below`, `sep` and `above` remain supported. These structural checks
do not independently verify external sources or establish that retained
provenance still describes modified cut points.
